text: The elegance of a theory tells us more than individual examples.
Language is, above all, a system with its own internal rules.
I take a claim seriously only once it has been tested in a sufficiently large data set.
To understand a sentence, I need to know who said it to whom and where.
An example that does not fit my theory makes the example, rather than the theory, suspect.
Phonetics, morphology and syntax can be studied independently of meaning and context.
Rather than trust my intuitions, I prefer measurement, surveys or experiments.
The social diversity of language—dialect, generation and social class—excites me more than language structure.
The most exciting part of a study is the model-building stage.
Grammar arises from the ways in which people use language.
Before formulating hypotheses in a new data set, I want to explore it and discover patterns.
The acquisition of language by children presupposes an innate structure.
Grammar should be explainable by a small number of general principles.
Word meanings cannot be fully given in a dictionary without looking at the situations in which they are used.
In an article, I look at the tables, statistics and supplementary materials first.
The best way to describe a language is to produce a complete inventory of its sounds and forms.
Unfinished sentences, hesitation and language mixing belong at the center of linguistics.
I enjoy resolving debates with constructed example sentences and thought experiments.
Noting interesting forms that do not fit a generalization is more valuable than writing theory.
Finding an element's place in the system is more instructive than counting how it is used.
